beginner: Lettuce likes loose, rich soil that drains well but never dries out completely. Because its roots are shallow and delicate, soggy or packed-down soil hurts lettuce more than it would a tomato, and letting the bed dry out even briefly makes the leaves turn bitter and the plant go to seed early. The simplest fix for almost any soil is to mix 2 to 3 inches of compost into the top few inches before you plant, which helps sandy soil hold water and helps heavy soil drain. Try to avoid thick clay, it forms a hard crust that small seedlings struggle to push through and stays wet around the roots.
seasoned: Lettuce is widely adaptable on the texture front, and although it produces well in almost any soil that drains freely, a fertile loam or sandy loam that stays high in organic matter and holds moisture well is where it does best. Its root system is shallow and fine, so it is far less forgiving of compaction and waterlogging than deeper-rooted crops, and consistent moisture is essential because even brief drought stress checks vegetative growth and pushes the plant toward bolting. Working 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before sowing improves both drainage on heavier soils and water retention on sandy ones. Heavy clay is the main texture to avoid, it crusts as seedlings emerge and holds water around the roots.

beginner: Soil pH measures acidity on a scale from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral and lower numbers are more acidic. Lettuce does best between 6.0 and 6.8, slightly acidic, because that is where the nutrients it needs are easiest for the roots to take up. If your soil is more acidic than 6.0 or more alkaline than 7.0, lettuce can show yellowing leaves or browning edges even when fertilizer is present. The only way to know your number is to test, so get an inexpensive soil test from your local extension office before adding lime to raise pH or sulfur to lower it.
seasoned: Soil pH governs nutrient availability, and lettuce is most productive in the slightly acidic 6.0 to 6.8 band where phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium stay soluble. Below about 6.0, calcium uptake falls off and aluminum and manganese grow more available, which can scorch leaf margins and stunt the fine root system. Above 7.0, iron and manganese begin to lock up and drive interveinal yellowing on new growth. Across the alkaline interior West and in alkaline-irrigation districts, growers often acidify before planting, while the naturally acidic soils of the forested East more often need lime to reach the target band.

beginner: Leafy crops run on nitrogen, the nutrient that drives the leaf growth you are harvesting, so feed a balanced or nitrogen-forward liquid fertilizer every 2 to 3 weeks. Keep it steady rather than heavy: a sudden big dose of nitrogen pushes fast, soft growth that can make tipburn worse (brown, dried edges on the inner leaves). And no amount of feeding stops bolting once heat and long days arrive, because that is driven by the plant's hormones, not by nutrients.
seasoned: Leafy crops run on nitrogen, which directly drives the tender leaf growth you're harvesting, so feed a balanced or nitrogen-forward liquid fertilizer every 2 to 3 weeks. Keep it steady rather than heavy: a sudden surge of nitrogen pushes fast, lush growth that can worsen tipburn by outrunning calcium delivery to the inner leaves. No amount of feeding prevents bolting once heat and long days arrive, since that is hormonal, not nutritional.

beginner: Lettuce likes a bit more nitrogen for quick, tender leaves. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the bed before planting at the label rate, then feed once more when the plants are a few inches tall. A small side-dressing of a nitrogen fertilizer, following the package rate for your row length, is plenty. Keep the fertilizer off the leaves and water it in.
seasoned: Lettuce responds to nitrogen for fast, tender growth. Work in a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 at about 2 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress nitrogen once plants are 3 to 4 inches tall, about 1 pound per 25 feet of row of 10-10-10 (UMN), or roughly a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row (USU). For tipburn-prone conditions favor a calcium-nitrate source over an ammonium-based one.

beginner: For lettuce, companion planting is mostly about sharing space well, not about one plant protecting another. Its best neighbors are crops that do not compete with it for the same room: fast radishes and deep-rooted carrots, plus chives, whose oniony smell helps hide lettuce from aphids. A lot of the popular "never plant these together" pairings for lettuce are old garden lore with mixed or no real evidence, so we keep those out of the way in the seasoned view. Get sun, water, and spacing right first. Companions are a small bonus on top.
seasoned: Lettuce companions are mostly about sharing space, not chemistry. Its best partners are fast or deep-rooted crops it does not compete with (radishes, carrots) and scent plants that help mask it from aphids (chives). Many popular 'avoid' pairings for lettuce are traditional lore with conflicting evidence rather than documented harm, so we keep those in the seasoned view with honest framing. Get sun, water, and spacing right first, companions are a small bonus on top.

beginner: Radishes grow fast and come out of the bed before the lettuce needs the room, so the two share space well. Their roots also loosen the soil a little for the lettuce. This is about saving space, not keeping pests away.
seasoned: Fast-maturing relay crop: radishes are harvested before lettuce fills the bed, and their taproots loosen surface compaction for lettuce's shallow roots. A space-saving pairing, not a pest control one.

beginner: Lettuce roots stay near the surface and carrots root deep, so the two do not fight for the same space underground and can grow side by side.
seasoned: Different root zones: lettuce is a shallow-rooted light feeder and carrots send a taproot deep, so the two share a bed without competing underground.

beginner: The oniony smell of chives can help hide lettuce from aphids, which find plants by scent. It helps a little rather than solving the problem on its own, so plant chives as a border around the bed.
seasoned: Allium scent compounds help mask lettuce from aphids that locate hosts by smell. A supporting deterrent, not a standalone fix, plant chives as a border row.

seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.

Encourage helpful insects like ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps, which keep small infestations in check on their own.

Plant flowers like marigolds and nasturtiums nearby, and grow some dill or cilantro too, whose flowers feed the helpful wasps and predators that do most of the real control.

Interplant flowers such as marigolds and nasturtiums, and grow some umbellifers like dill or cilantro nearby, whose flowers feed the parasitic wasps and predators that do most of the real control.

seasoned: Several aphid species feed on leafy greens, most commonly the green peach aphid. Through the growing season they reproduce asexually, so a few founders become dense colonies within days once temperatures warm and growth is soft and lush.

beginner: Set beer traps with the rim level with the soil so the slugs fall in and cannot climb out, and refresh them every couple of days. Sprinkle diatomaceous earth in a ring around vulnerable plants, but remember it stops working once it gets wet and needs reapplying after rain or watering. Hand-pick them after dark with a flashlight, when they are out feeding. An iron-phosphate bait (sold as Sluggo and similar) is approved for organic gardens and safe around pets and wildlife; it stops the slugs feeding so they die within a few days. Scatter it in the evening after watering, when slugs are most active, for the best results.

beginner: Pull mulch back from around seedlings and clear away the boards, pots, and leaf litter near the bed that give slugs a daytime hiding spot. A bare, raked strip around the planting slows them down on their way in. Encourage ground beetles, and hedgehogs if you have them, since both hunt slugs through the night.
seasoned: Pull mulch back from around seedlings and clear the boards, pots, and leaf litter that give slugs a daytime hiding place close to the bed. A bare, cultivated strip around the planting slows their approach. Encourage ground beetles and, if you have them, hedgehogs, which prey on slugs through the night.

beginner: Slugs and snails feed mostly at night and in cool, damp weather, rasping ragged holes in tender leaves and shearing off young seedlings completely. The damage is worst in wet spells and in beds with damp mulch or debris that give them somewhere to hide during the day.
seasoned: Slugs and snails feed mostly at night and in the cool, damp hours, rasping irregular holes through tender leaves and shearing off young seedlings entirely. Damage is heaviest in wet spells and in beds with damp mulch or debris that give them daytime shelter.

beginner: Plants wilt in the heat of the day and just fail to thrive even though you are watering steadily, then slowly decline with no obvious cause above ground. Lift a struggling plant and you find clusters of aphids on the roots under a mass of white, woolly wax. It is easy to mistake for drought or a root disease until you look below the soil.
seasoned: Plants wilt during the heat of the day and fail to thrive despite steady watering, then decline with no obvious cause above ground. Lift a suspect plant and you find clusters of the aphids on the roots under masses of white, woolly wax. The damage is easy to mistake for drought or root disease until you look below the soil.

beginner: Once the aphids are on the roots, no spray will rescue the crop, so the fix is about how you manage the planting rather than treating it. Pull up and remove badly affected plants. Where it has happened, dig the soil over deeply and let it dry out thoroughly before planting lettuce there again, and keep your plants unstressed and well watered so a fast-growing crop can often still finish acceptably.

Where the problem has occurred, work the soil deeply and let it dry thoroughly before replanting lettuce there, and keep plants unstressed and well watered so a fast-growing crop can often still finish acceptably.

beginner: Move lettuce around so it does not come back to the same ground each season, and avoid planting it close to Lombardy poplar trees, which are where the aphid spends the winter. Some lettuce varieties are bred to resist root aphid and are worth looking for if this pest keeps showing up in your garden.
seasoned: Rotate lettuce so it does not return to the same ground each season, and avoid planting it close to Lombardy poplars, the aphid's overwintering host. Some lettuce varieties carry resistance to root aphid and are worth seeking out if the pest is a recurring problem in your garden.

beginner: The lettuce root aphid feeds on lettuce roots out of sight. It spends winter as eggs on Lombardy poplar trees, then winged ones fly to lettuce in early summer, which is why the problem is worst where lettuce grows near those trees.
seasoned: The lettuce root aphid, Pemphigus bursarius, feeds on lettuce roots out of sight. It spends winter as eggs on Lombardy poplar, then winged forms migrate to lettuce in early summer, which is why infestations are worst where lettuce grows near those trees.

beginner: Pale yellow patches show up on the upper side of the older leaves first, with a downy gray-purple mold underneath them. In cool, wet weather it spreads fast, and the affected areas turn brown and die as it moves up the plant.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches appear on the upper surface of older leaves first, matched underneath by a downy gray-purple mold. In cool, wet weather it spreads fast, and affected areas brown and die as the infection moves up the plant.

beginner: Remove and throw away affected leaves right away, and open the planting up so air moves through and the leaves dry faster. A copper-based spray can help if you use it before the disease takes hold, as a preventive, rather than trying to cure it once it has spread.
seasoned: Remove and dispose of affected leaves promptly, and open the planting up to improve airflow so leaves dry faster. A copper-based fungicide can help when used preventively, before the disease takes hold, rather than as a cure once it has spread.

beginner: Water at the soil and early in the day so the leaves are not wet overnight, since wet leaves are what this disease needs. Space plants well apart for airflow, and choose resistant varieties, which extension programs rate as the single most effective control. Avoid growing lettuce under cover through fall and winter without good airflow, where the cool, still, humid air is just what the disease likes.
seasoned: Water at soil level and early in the day so leaves are not wet overnight, since leaf wetness is what the pathogen needs. Space plants generously for airflow, and choose resistant varieties, which extension programs rate as the single most effective control. Avoid growing under cover through autumn and winter without good ventilation, where the cool, still, humid air is ideal for it.

beginner: Downy mildew is caused by an organism called Bremia lactucae, a water mold rather than a true fungus. It needs cool, damp conditions and water sitting on the leaves to take hold, and its spores blow on the wind and spread quickly during wet spells. It does not survive in the soil, and because it is not a true fungus, ordinary fungus sprays may not work against it.
seasoned: Downy mildew is caused by Bremia lactucae, an oomycete (a water mold, not a true fungus). It needs cool, damp conditions and water sitting on the leaves to take hold, and its wind-borne spores spread quickly during moist spells. It does not survive in the soil, and because it is not a true fungus, ordinary fungicides aimed at fungi may not touch it.

beginner: Brown, papery scorch appears along the edges of the inner leaves, down in the heart of the plant rather than on the outer leaves. It does not spread from plant to plant, and it shows up most in romaine types and in hot weather.

beginner: Tipburn is a growing problem rather than a disease, and it is rarely about a lack of calcium in the soil. Calcium moves through the plant in the stream of water it pulls up and releases through its leaves, so it ends up in the outer leaves that release the most water. The young inner leaves are tucked inside the head where the air is still and humid, so they release very little water and, during fast growth, cannot pull in enough calcium, and their edges collapse. Heat and lush, fast growth make it worse.
seasoned: Tipburn is a physiological disorder, not a disease, and it is rarely about low calcium in the soil. Calcium travels through the plant in the stream of water it pulls up and transpires, so it collects in the fast-transpiring outer leaves. The young inner leaves are enclosed in the head where the air is still and humid and they transpire very little, so during rapid growth they cannot draw enough calcium and their edges collapse. Heat and lush, fast growth make it worse.

Because the roots are shallow and sit in just the top few inches of soil, lettuce dries out easily, and even short dry spells stress it quickly. Steady, even moisture also helps the plant move calcium to the fast-growing inner leaves, which prevents tipburn (the brown, dried leaf edges).

If you do water from above, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off before the cool, damp evening, when leaf diseases are most likely to take hold.

Dry stress also makes the plant bolt sooner, and once it bolts the leaves turn bitter.

beginner: Drainage holes are a must, and the roots must never sit in standing water: waterlogged soil leaves no air for the roots and invites root rot, which lettuce rarely recovers from. If you use a saucer under the pot, empty it after each watering and after rain, or raise the pot up on feet, bricks, or slats so it is not sitting in a puddle or flat on concrete.
